m: Published list figure, priced at 1 March 2026 close
did: Started Future Mining in 1994 doing contract gold-shaft cleaning, then from 1997 bought AngloGold's marginal Vaal Reefs shafts and rolled them into African Rainbow Minerals; later added Sanlam and African Rainbow Capital stakes worth about $2.7bn on the JSE in 2026.
why: The 2002 Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act converted mineral rights to state custodianship and required black ownership to renew them, so majors needed a credible black-owned counterparty. Motsepe already had operating shafts, so he was the buyer with an operating record rather than a shell.
obst: Banks would not lend to a black-owned mining start-up in 1994, so he bought shafts with no upfront cash on profit-share terms and paid from cash flow. The gold price then fell to about $253 an ounce in 1999, which is exactly why the majors were selling.
turn: The 1997 purchase of AngloGold's loss-making Vaal Reefs shafts, run profitably on a low-cost, union-agreed profit-share model.

m: Published list figure; cross-checked against an 11.39 percent Capitec stake valued at $3.7bn by Billionaires.Africa in Feb 2026
did: Left Boland Bank and in 2000 founded Capitec with Riaan Stassen and PSG backing, rolling up micro-lending branches into a full bank in 2001 and building a single low-fee transactional account for wage earners the big four would not serve.
why: South Africa's big four priced retail accounts on bundled fees and branch cost, leaving 15 million wage earners on cash. Capitec ran one product, paperless account opening, biometric ID and long branch hours, so its cost to serve was a fraction of Absa's and it could price transparently and still make money.
obst: The 2012-14 unsecured lending crisis and African Bank's 2014 collapse tarred every mass-market lender; then Viceroy Research's January 2020 short report alleged reckless lending and the shares fell about 20 percent in a day before the Reserve Bank publicly rejected the claims.
turn: Winning a full banking licence in 2001 and converting a micro-lending branch network into a deposit-taking bank.

m: Published list figure; his direct Naspers holding alone was valued at $420m by Billionaires.Africa in Feb 2026
did: Co-founded M-Net in 1985 as Africa's first pay-TV service, then as Naspers CEO from 1997 to 2014 bought 46.5 percent of an unknown Chinese messaging startup, Tencent, for about $32m in 2001 and refused to sell it down.
why: He took no salary or bonus for 17 years, only share options, so his pay was a leveraged call on the Tencent position and he could not take profits early. Naspers was also an Afrikaans newspaper group with no reason to be in Chinese messaging, which is why nobody bid against him in 2001.
comp: later Softbank and Tencent's own backers
obst: Naspers carried the reputational debt of having been the National Party's newspaper group under apartheid, which limited its international deal access; and the 2001 dot-com bust left it with very little capital at exactly the moment the Tencent stake was on offer.
turn: The $32m purchase of a controlling stake in Tencent in 2001, at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

m: Published list figure
did: Took over his father's Dar es Salaam trading house in 1999 and converted it from importing to manufacturing, buying privatised state textile, edible oil and flour mills and rebuilding them; METL now makes soap, cooking oil, flour, textiles and beverages across a dozen African countries.
why: Tanzania's 1990s privatisation dumped loss-making parastatal factories at scrap prices because nobody would take the labour liabilities. Dewji bought them, and because local manufacture sat behind the East African Community external tariff, his goods undercut the imports his family had sold.
obst: He was kidnapped at gunpoint outside a Dar es Salaam hotel gym in October 2018 and held for nine days; the group also had to absorb Tanzania's abrupt 2016-20 tax enforcement drive and repeated shilling devaluations against dollar-priced input costs.
turn: The early-2000s decision to stop trading and start owning the mills, beginning with rehabilitated privatised textile and edible-oil plants.

m: Published list figure
did: Quit a state telecoms engineering job, built electrical contractor Retrofit, then fought a five-year constitutional case against Zimbabwe's state telecom monopoly, won in the Supreme Court in December 1997, launched Econet Wireless in 1998 and later built Liquid Telecom's pan-African fibre backbone.
why: The litigation itself was the asset. By striking down the PTC monopoly on free-expression grounds he created the licence he then won, in a country with well under 100,000 fixed lines. First-mover mobile with no incumbent distribution meant Econet took the subscriber base before foreign operators arrived.
obst: The Mugabe government refused him the licence he had won, harassed and detained associates, and he left for South Africa in 2000 and then Britain. Later, hyperinflation destroyed Zimbabwean dollar revenue and Econet had to re-price in US dollars to survive.
turn: The December 1997 Supreme Court ruling that the state telecoms monopoly was unconstitutional.

m: Published list figure; his listed Shoprite, Brait and Invicta stakes were valued at $1.3bn by Billionaires.Africa in Feb 2026
did: Bought a struggling eight-store grocery chain called Shoprite for about R1m in 1979 and grew it into Africa's largest food retailer, while taking control of discount clothier Pepkor and pushing both into Zambia, Angola, Nigeria and Mozambique from the mid-1990s.
why: He aimed at the low-income and township customer that the established chains priced past, running no-frills stores on thin gross margin and huge volume. Expanding north from 1995 put modern grocery distribution into countries that had none, so Shoprite set the price floor before any competitor arrived.
obst: He sold Pepkor to Steinhoff in 2015 for shares rather than cash; when Steinhoff's accounting fraud broke in December 2017 the shares collapsed and several billion dollars of his fortune vanished. He sued Steinhoff for about R59bn and settled for a fraction.
turn: The 1979 purchase of the eight-store Shoprite chain for roughly R1 million.

m: Published list figure; includes proceeds of the December 2025 sale of his 77 percent Geregu holding, reported at about $750m
did: Founded Zenon Petroleum and Gas in 2003 and made it Nigeria's largest diesel supplier by owning tank farms and a tanker fleet, bought African Petroleum in 2007, then acquired the 435MW Geregu plant in the 2013 power privatisation, listed it on the NGX in 2022 and sold control to MA'AM Energy in December 2025.
why: Nigeria subsidised petrol but not diesel, so diesel was the one deregulated fuel where a private marketer could set price. Otedola bought the storage depots and vessels, which is where the margin actually sat, then repeated the trick on generation assets the state sold below replacement cost in 2013.
obst: The 2008-09 oil price crash and naira slide left Zenon with roughly $1.2bn of bank debt that ended up with AMCON; he fell off the Forbes billionaire list entirely and spent years working the debt down before re-emerging through Forte Oil and Geregu.
turn: Winning the 435MW Geregu plant in the 2013 PHCN privatisation, the asset he eventually sold for about $750m.

m: Third-party estimate of the Billon family agro-industrial fortune; no separate personal figure is published
did: Ran SIFCA as chief executive from 2000 to 2012, the group his father Pierre helped found in 1964; it now turns over about $800m through PalmCI in palm oil, SAPH in rubber and SucriVoire in sugar, employs over 33,000 people and buys from more than 110,000 smallholders.
why: When Côte d'Ivoire privatised the state palm monopoly Palmindustrie from 1997, SIFCA was the only Ivorian group with the mills and the smallholder relationships to absorb it, so it bought the plantations rather than a foreign trader. Owning the crush and the refinery captured the margin the state had given away.
obst: The 2002-2011 civil war split the country and put western plantations inside the conflict zone, and the 2010-11 post-election crisis closed Abidjan port and the banking system for months. SIFCA also had to restructure heavy debt after the 2008 commodity swing.
turn: Acquiring the privatised Palmindustrie assets and folding them into PalmCI, which made SIFCA the dominant Ivorian palm processor.

m: Dated published figure, not refreshed by Forbes since 2020; Famfa's carried interest in OML 127 is unlisted
did: Worked as a bank secretary, ran the fashion label Supreme Stitches from 1985, then in 1993 was awarded oil prospecting licence OPL 216 offshore Nigeria, farmed it out to Star Deep and Texaco to carry the drilling, and ended up with a stake in the Agbami field, which began producing in 2008.
why: The 1990s indigenous allocation round handed deepwater acreage to Nigerian-owned companies that had no capacity to drill it. The value was in farming the block out to a major who bore all the capital cost while Famfa retained a carried interest, so the fortune came from holding a licence, not from operating.
obst: In 2000 the Obasanjo government stripped 50 percent of Famfa's interest and reassigned it to NNPC. She litigated for twelve years, and only in 2012 did the Supreme Court of Nigeria confirm Famfa's 60 percent interest in OML 127.
turn: The 2012 Supreme Court judgment restoring Famfa's stripped interest in OML 127, just as Agbami hit plateau production.

s: Forbes Africa valuation cited by Billionaires.Africa, 2025-2026
m: Third-party estimate of about 547bn CFA francs across unlisted holdings; no exchange-listed stakes to verify against
did: Began as a truck driver in Cameroon's North West, moved into transport and then tea, building Ndawara into the largest privately held tea plantation in West Africa alongside a cattle ranch, Douala and Yaoundé commercial property, South African real estate and 30 percent of mobile operator Nexttel.
why: In 1980s Cameroon the binding constraint was access to import licences and bank credit, not demand. He converted that access into hard, inflation-proof assets - land, tea bushes, cattle and buildings - rather than trading stock, so the fortune survived the CFA franc's 50 percent devaluation in 1994.
obst: In 2022-23 South African lenders seized and auctioned his Johannesburg and Sandton properties over a disputed loan, triggering a diplomatic row and Cameroonian retaliation against South African firms; Nexttel has also been locked in years of shareholder conflict with its Vietnamese partner Viettel.
turn: Taking over the Ndawara highlands and turning a marginal state tea concession into West Africa's largest private plantation.

m: Modelled: disclosed Zenith Bank holding valued at $643m in June 2026 plus unlisted Quantum Capital, Cyberspace and Lagos property
did: Founded Zenith Bank in May 1990 with about N20m of capital and built it into Nigeria's largest bank by tier-one capital, computerising branches years before rivals, then added Visafone, sold to MTN in 2015, and Quantum Capital. He stepped down as chairman in May 2026 under the CBN tenure rule.
why: The post-1986 licensing wave created scores of undercapitalised banks competing on relationships. Ovia competed on settlement speed instead, wiring branches together early, which won the oil-sector deposits that fund cheap. When the CBN raised minimum capital in 2004, Zenith was a consolidator, not a target.
obst: The 2004-05 recapitalisation directive cut Nigeria's banks from 89 to 25 and killed most of his founding cohort; the 2009 Sanusi audit then wiped out several survivors. He also had to unwind non-bank subsidiaries after the CBN's 2010 repeal of universal banking.
turn: The CBN's 2004 order to raise minimum capital to N25bn, which turned Zenith from one of many into one of the few.

m: Dated published figure of $800m; later third-party estimates run to $1.2bn but rest on unlisted Kampala property with no public valuation
did: Returned to Uganda in 1985 with about GBP 25,000 saved from London jobs, opened one of the first licensed forex bureaux, founded Crane Bank in 1995, and assembled a Kampala portfolio of office blocks, hotels, schools, insurance and the Rosebud cut-flower export business.
why: Museveni's 1993 Expropriated Properties Act let Ugandan Asians reclaim or buy back property seized by Idi Amin in 1972. Nobody else wanted central Kampala buildings with contested title and no tenants, so he bought them at distressed prices and the liberalised forex trade generated the cash to do it.
comp: Stanbic Uganda and Barclays (against Crane Bank)
obst: His family was expelled by Idi Amin in 1972 and he arrived in Britain with nothing. Later, the Bank of Uganda seized Crane Bank in October 2016 as undercapitalised and sold it to DFCU; the resulting litigation ran for years before the courts largely cleared him.
turn: The 1993 Expropriated Properties Act, which let him buy back central Kampala real estate almost nobody else would bid for.

m: Inferred from the $575m Thawte sale in 1999 plus an unlisted Canonical whose revenue reached about $250m in 2023; no published mark
did: Founded certificate authority Thawte in a Cape Town garage in 1995, got its root certificate trusted by Netscape and Microsoft, and sold it to VeriSign in December 1999 for about $575m; founded Canonical in 2004 and shipped Ubuntu, now the dominant Linux distribution in public cloud.
why: US export controls on strong cryptography meant an American certificate authority could not legally sell 128-bit certificates abroad. Being in South Africa was the whole edge: Thawte was outside US jurisdiction, so it took the non-US web-server certificate market before VeriSign was allowed to compete for it.
comp: later Red Hat, SUSE and Amazon Linux against Ubuntu
obst: South African exchange controls made expatriating the Thawte proceeds costly and he left the country to do it. Canonical then ran on his own capital for over a decade, and the Ubuntu Phone and Unity desktop projects were killed in 2017 after years of spending, with about 80 jobs cut.
turn: Netscape's 1996 decision to bundle Thawte's root certificate, which made a South African startup a globally trusted CA overnight.

s: Forbes Africa's 50 Richest 2015 ($500m); Kenyan press estimates near KSh100bn in 2025
m: Dated Forbes figure updated by third-party Kenyan estimates; Devki is unlisted with turnover reported above $600m
did: Arrived in Kenya from Gujarat in 1979 aged seventeen to work as a Hindu priest, moved into a hardware shop, started Devki Steel Mills in 1988 rolling roofing sheets, then launched National Cement and the Simba Cement brand in 2010 and built a clinker plant to stop importing.
why: Backward integration under tariff cover. The East African Community external tariff on finished steel and cement made local production structurally cheaper than imports, and his own clinker line removed the biggest imported input cost, so he undercut Bamburi and East African Portland on landed price.
obst: Cheap imported clinker from Egypt and Asia repeatedly squeezed margins; ARM Cement's 2018 collapse into administration destabilised the whole Kenyan sector; and the 2016 interest-rate cap froze Kenyan bank lending to industrial borrowers just as he was funding new kilns.
turn: The 2010 move out of steel into cement with the Athi River grinding plant that became Simba Cement.

s: Billionaires.Africa valuation of the Bidco group at about $700m, 2025
m: Modelled from an unlisted family group valuation; Forbes listed him at $1.6bn in 2013 and has since dropped him, so the earlier figure is not used
did: Joined his father's Nairobi business in 1985 as it moved from garments into edible oils, took over as chief executive in the early 1990s, and in 2002 bought Unilever's Kenyan edible-oils business with the Kimbo, Cowboy and Elianto brands, making Bidco East Africa's largest cooking-oil manufacturer.
why: Rather than fight the multinational incumbent on shelf, he bought its brands outright, acquiring fifty years of consumer habit in a single transaction. He then integrated backwards into palm cultivation in Uganda so the raw material was internal, which is what let Bidco hold price through import-cost swings.
obst: The Kalangala oil palm project in Uganda drew years of land-rights litigation and NGO campaigns over displaced islanders; Bidco also fought protracted tax assessments with the Kenya Revenue Authority and a persistent counterfeit-packaging problem in its core brands.
turn: The 2002 acquisition of Unilever's Kenyan edible-oils business and its brand portfolio.

m: Modelled: disclosed 1.76 percent FirstRand holding valued at $467m at Feb 2026 prices; excludes unlisted assets
did: Put up R10,000 each with GT Ferreira and Pat Goss to start Rand Consolidated Investments in 1977, reverse-took-over Rand Merchant Bank in 1985, bought Momentum Life in 1992 and merged the group with First National Bank in 1998 to create FirstRand, still one of Africa's largest banking groups.
why: The trio exploited a regulatory seam in 1970s South African leasing and discounting that the clearing banks were not structured to work, then compounded it by using listed paper to reverse into bigger, sleepier balance sheets rather than growing organically. Each takeover was paid for in shares they had just re-rated.
obst: The 1985 debt standstill, when P.W. Botha's Rubicon speech triggered capital flight and South Africa suspended foreign debt repayments, hit exactly as they were absorbing Rand Merchant Bank; sanctions then kept the group locked out of international funding for the rest of the decade.
turn: The 1985 reverse takeover of Rand Merchant Bank, which gave a small finance house a banking licence and a brand.

m: Modelled: 12.5 percent Aspen Pharmacare holding valued at $418m at Feb 2026 prices
did: Sold generics distributor Covan Zurich to South African Druggists in 1997 for about R150m, then with Gus Attridge bought a small pharmaceutical company the same year and built Aspen into the southern hemisphere's largest generics maker by acquiring end-of-life molecules from GSK, AstraZeneca and MSD.
why: Big pharma wanted out of off-patent products too small for its sales force but still cash-generative. Aspen bought them at low multiples and ran them on a South African cost base, so a molecule that was marginal inside GSK was highly profitable inside Aspen. The 1997 Medicines Act supplied local volume.
obst: Aspen's bid for Adcock Ingram collapsed in 2014 on regulatory and political resistance; European and Italian competition authorities then investigated its cancer-drug pricing from 2016, and a 2018 analyst attack on its accounting and debt load knocked more than half off the share price.
turn: The 2001 licence from GlaxoSmithKline and Boehringer Ingelheim to manufacture generic antiretrovirals for Africa.

m: Third-party estimate of about $420m, described by the publisher as the combined market value of her real estate holdings rather than a verified figure
did: Lost a fishing business at 25 and was left roughly $2.5m in debt, went back to university for an MBA, then incorporated Manet Housing in 1994 and delivered over 1,800 homes across Accra plus the Manet Twin Towers office blocks in Airport City and a resort at Ada.
why: Ghanaian mortgage finance barely existed and cedi lending rates ran well above 25 percent, so local developers could not fund construction. She pre-sold units in dollars to the diaspora, financing each phase off customer deposits instead of bank debt and immunising the balance sheet against devaluation.
obst: The collapse of her fishing venture left her personally indebted before she had any property assets. Later, the 2022 cedi crash and Ghana's sovereign debt default destroyed local-currency mortgage demand and pushed imported building materials up sharply.
turn: Abandoning fishing for housing and selling to the diaspora in hard currency, which turned a debt-laden founder into a self-funding developer.

s: Billionaires.Africa, 2025 estimate; Forbes listed him at $500m in 2013
m: Third-party estimate of an unlisted group; published figures range from $400m to $800m and the low end is used
did: Left school at fourteen and started selling potato crisps and ice cream in Dar es Salaam in 1973, opened the Azam flour mill in the mid-1980s, then built out bakeries, Azam Cola and juices, the Azam Marine ferries on the Dar-Zanzibar route, petroleum and Azam TV, now across eleven countries.
why: Tanzania's socialist era gave the state National Milling Corporation a grain monopoly it could not service. When milling was deregulated he put private capacity next to the port and imported wheat directly, controlling both landed cost and mill, then used flour cash flow to buy trucks, ferries and bottling lines.
obst: He built through years of Tanzanian import licensing controls and foreign-exchange rationing that made buying wheat abroad a bureaucratic ordeal; the 2022 wheat price spike after Russia's invasion of Ukraine hit his single largest input with no hedge available locally.
turn: Opening the Azam flour mill in the mid-1980s as Tanzania dismantled the state grain-milling monopoly.

m: Modelled: 13.5 percent Seplat Energy holding valued at $372m at late-January 2026 prices; excludes unlisted Petrolin assets
did: A petroleum engineer who worked in Gabon before founding the Petrolin Group in 1992 as an oil trading and advisory house, he became the third major shareholder behind Seplat Energy, the indigenous Nigerian producer that bought Shell, Total and Agip's 45 percent of OMLs 4, 38 and 41 in 2010.
why: Between 2010 and 2015 the majors sold onshore Niger Delta blocks cheaply because sabotage, spills and community litigation made them unmanageable for a listed supermajor. Indigenous consortiums that could handle host communities bought producing barrels at a fraction of international per-barrel prices.
obst: The Niger Delta Avengers blew up the Forcados export line in February 2016 and shut Seplat's main evacuation route for most of a year, pushing the company into loss. He has also spent years in dispute with the Beninese state over the Sèmè port and rail concession.
turn: Backing Seplat's 2010 purchase of Shell's OML 4, 38 and 41 stake, then its dual London and Lagos listing in April 2014.

m: Modelled floor: disclosed Wema Bank and Vitafoam stakes valued above $300m in July 2026, plus unlisted Premier Lotto and a 69.9 percent Arbico holding
did: Founded Premier Lotto in Lagos in 1977 and turned street numbers-betting into a licensed franchise running through more than 200 principal agents and roughly 16,000 retail kiosks; he also owns 69.9 percent of construction firm Arbico and a Wema Bank stake worth about $291m.
why: He formalised an informal cash game. In a country with almost no consumer credit or bank penetration, a daily draw settled in cash through franchised agents needed no infrastructure, collected float every day and compounded for four decades without ever raising outside capital.
comp: state-run lotteries in the south west
obst: The National Lottery Regulatory Commission repeatedly tried to bring lottery under exclusive federal licensing, a fight settled only when the Supreme Court held that lottery is a residual state matter; the 2020 Lagos covid lockdown also shut the kiosk network that is the entire distribution system.
turn: The 1977 launch of the franchised agent model that put Baba Ijebu kiosks on every commercial street in south-west Nigeria.

s: Billionaires.Africa and South African press estimates, 2023-2025
m: Third-party estimates spanning roughly $200m to $270m; assets are largely unlisted so the midpoint is used
did: Daughter of Liberty Life founder Donald Gordon, she was deputy chair of Liberty Investors, co-founded Women's Investment Portfolio Holdings in 1994 and took it to a JSE listing in 1999 as the first women-owned company to list there, and in 2003 bought the De Morgenzon wine estate in Stellenbosch.
why: Post-1994 empowerment codes made black and women shareholders a licensing and procurement requirement for South African corporates, which created genuine demand for a credible women-owned investment vehicle. WIPHOLD was structured as a broad-based holder rather than a front, which is why corporates would deal with it.
obst: Banks would not finance a women-only investment consortium in 1994, so WIPHOLD raised its founding capital from thousands of rural women through savings groups instead. She has since spent years publicly fighting fronting arrangements and, in a long-running case, a Cape auctioneer and the financial regulators.
turn: WIPHOLD's 1999 listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

m: Modelled: 8.337 percent Seplat Energy holding valued at $229m at late-January 2026 prices
did: A geologist from NNPC and Allied Energy, he co-founded Platform Petroleum in 2002 to work the Egbaoma marginal field, then co-founded Seplat with A.B.C. Orjiako in 2009; Seplat bought 45 percent of OMLs 4, 38 and 41 from Shell, Total and Agip in 2010 for $340m and he ran it as chief executive until 2020.
why: Nigeria's 2003 marginal field awards gave Nigerian geologists fields the majors had written off, which is how a salaried technical man acquired reserves without capital. That operating record is what qualified Seplat as a buyer when the majors began divesting producing onshore acreage from 2010.
obst: The Niger Delta Avengers destroyed the Forcados export line in February 2016, cutting Seplat's main evacuation route for around fifteen months and pushing the company to a loss; the 2015-17 naira devaluations and NNPC cash-call arrears hit at the same time.
turn: The 2010 acquisition of Shell's OML 4, 38 and 41 interest, which took Seplat from a marginal-field operator to a producer of scale.

s: Third-party 2026 estimates of over $200m; Flutterwave valued at $3.3bn by Ripple's June 2026 investment (Bloomberg)
m: Modelled from a founder stake in a private company whose size is undisclosed, against a reported $3.3bn valuation
did: Co-founded Flutterwave in 2016 after engineering roles at Standard Bank, PayPal and Google, building a single payments API on top of dozens of incompatible African bank switches and mobile money rails; it raised $250m in February 2022 at over $3bn and took a Ripple equity investment in June 2026 at $3.3bn.
why: Africa has more than 40 currencies and dozens of national bank switches that do not talk to each other, so selling across borders meant a separate integration and licence per country. Flutterwave did the licensing and settlement work itself and sold one endpoint, regulatory labour rivals could not shortcut.
obst: In April 2022 Kenya's High Court froze about $52m across Flutterwave accounts on money-laundering allegations, a case the authorities later withdrew in 2023; the company also faced internal misconduct allegations and heightened Central Bank of Nigeria licensing scrutiny in the same period.
turn: The February 2022 $250m Series D, which tripled the valuation past $3bn and made it Africa's most valuable startup.

s: Third-party estimates around $200m; Visa's Nov 2019 purchase of 20 percent valued Interswitch at $1bn
m: Modelled from an undisclosed founder stake in a private company against the 2019 unicorn valuation and the 2022 $110m round
did: Founded Interswitch in 2002 to build Nigeria's interbank transaction switch when cheques still took weeks to clear, then launched the Verve card in 2009 and the Quickteller payments platform; Visa bought 20 percent in November 2019 at a $1bn valuation, making it Africa's first fintech unicorn.
why: He built the shared switching layer before the regulator required one, so when the Central Bank of Nigeria's 2012 cashless policy forced electronic settlement, every bank and ATM already routed through his rails. That is a toll on interbank volume, not a product a better app can displace.
obst: A London listing was prepared and shelved twice, in 2016 and again around 2019-2022, each time derailed by Nigeria's foreign-exchange crisis and naira devaluation, which wrecked the dollar comparables. The bank-owned NIBSS also built competing rails with regulatory backing.
turn: Visa's November 2019 investment for 20 percent at a $1bn valuation.

m: Modelled: 4.26 percent Aspen Pharmacare holding valued at $142m at Feb 2026 prices
did: A chartered accountant who co-founded Aspen Pharmacare with Stephen Saad in 1997 and served as deputy chief executive until 2021, he ran the acquisition and integration machine that absorbed more than thirty acquired product portfolios and built out the Port Elizabeth sterile manufacturing complex.
why: Aspen's model only worked if acquired molecules could be transferred into South African plants fast and cheaply; the value was created in technology transfer and plant qualification, not in the purchase price. Attridge's job was making a dozen bought portfolios behave like one manufacturing base.
obst: European and Italian competition authorities investigated Aspen's cancer-drug pricing from 2016, forcing price cuts; in 2018 an analyst assault on the group's accounting and its heavy acquisition debt roughly halved the share price and forced disposals of the infant nutrition and Japanese businesses.
turn: The 2008-09 acquisition of a GSK product portfolio that also left GSK holding about 16 percent of Aspen, giving the company a multinational partner and pipeline.

m: Modelled: 38.25 percent indirect Oando holding valued at $132m at late-January 2026 prices
did: A lawyer who founded oil trader Ocean and Oil in 1994, took control of the privatised Unipetrol in 2000-2002, merged it with Agip Nigeria to form Oando in 2003, listed in Johannesburg in 2005, bought ConocoPhillips' Nigerian upstream for about $1.5bn in 2014 and Eni's onshore NAOC JV for roughly $783m in 2024.
why: The 2000 downstream privatisation sold state fuel marketers with depots and retail sites at book value, giving him a listed vehicle and cash flow. He then used that listed paper and reserve-based debt to buy upstream assets when the majors exited onshore Nigeria under community and sabotage pressure.
obst: The $1.5bn ConocoPhillips purchase closed in 2014 just as Brent fell from $110 to under $30, leaving roughly $2.5bn of debt against collapsed cash flow; Nigeria's SEC then suspended Oando's shares in 2017, ordered a forensic audit and moved to remove him, a sanction only unwound through a 2019-2021 settlement.
turn: The 2014 acquisition of ConocoPhillips' Nigerian business, which converted a fuel marketer into an oil producer and nearly destroyed the company doing it.

m: Modelled: 47.22 percent holding in Caxton and CTP Publishers and Printers valued at $124m at Feb 2026 prices
co: Caxton and CTP Publishers and Printers
did: Built CTP with Noel Coburn from a printing base, took over the Caxton publishing group in 1985 and merged with Perskor in 1998, assembling South Africa's largest commercial printing operation alongside a network of dozens of free community newspapers and consumer magazines.
why: Free local newspapers were unattractive to the national press groups because they carried no cover price, but they were the only medium for small-town retail advertising and they filled his own gravure presses. Owning titles and presses meant high plant utilisation and near-zero marginal newspaper cost.
obst: Print advertising revenue in South Africa fell steadily from around 2010 as classifieds moved online, and the group fought and largely blocked Media24's attempt to consolidate the printing market, in a competition process that ran for years while its own core market shrank.
turn: The 1998 merger with Perskor, which combined the country's two big Afrikaans-rooted print and publishing operations under his control.
